Name: Roope Pöyry
aboutMeContent:
Lead Developer with almost 10 years of experience, working where architecture meets product. AI now writes most of my code, so my work is deciding what to build, designing the data model and the UI, and building the review and tooling that let a small team ship fast without losing control.

I match human review to the stakes. In payroll rules, data models and production changes I still read the diff; a family app can rest on a spec, tests and a browser check. Years of hands-on React, .NET and Azure are what let me judge the code an agent writes.

content.EasyOpp:
I lead architecture and engineering at EasyOpp, on a work-time and fleet management platform. In a small team I also own production and much of the product design: deployments, the Azure footprint, the database and incident triage, and the redesign and scoping of features customers use every day. Since 2026 Claude Code has written most of my code; my part is the design, the review and quality system around it, and running what ships.

Platform and reliability
  • Azure subscription migration with zero downtime. Planned and carried out, alone, a move of the whole Azure footprint to a new subscription: rehearsed on dev and test, run in parallel and validated against real production data before the DNS swap. No customer-visible downtime.
  • Finding the real database bottleneck. Production was slow while average load sat under 8%. Metrics showed the hot tables no longer fit in memory, with about twenty times more time spent waiting on disk than on CPU, so the fix was a tier sized for IO, proven first on a dev canary.
  • Gated legacy retirement. Removed several legacy services and code paths, more than 150,000 lines, each by flipping the default, watching, and only then deleting. Moving webhook ingest to Azure Functions the same way exposed a race that could open two work-time records for one driver; the fix went into the schema as a unique index.

Product
  • Configurable payroll calculation engine. Sole maintainer since the 2024 redesign. Customers on several Finnish collective labor agreements share one engine with no per-agreement code, and new rules, such as tiered paid breaks and weekly overtime counted by workdays, arrive as settings rather than forks.
  • Shift planning. Recurring shifts expand at read time, so "every Tuesday forever" is one row, and the design has needed almost no maintenance since launch. Newer work is for the planners who still use Excel: a compact, spreadsheet-like table view, and shift templates that make recurring shifts simpler.
  • UI redesigns. Moved the web and mobile apps onto shared design tokens with a dark theme, and redesigned the work-time front page, the calculation settings and the reporting tool, which gained ready-made presets and a simpler UI. Each started as a Claude mockup.

Engineering with AI
  • Review and quality system. Designed and tuned the team's staged review flow, which settles a change's structure before anyone reads its lines and hands a person a prepared approval, with as many stages as the stakes call for. Conventions became checks in the build and tests, so new code meets each rule from day one and old debt is counted down.
  • AI for the whole company, with guardrails. Customer service and onboarding asked for a way to see why a feature behaves as it does, and to debug it when it doesn't. That used to mean a Slack question that a developer pasted into Claude Code, then pasted the answer back. Now they ask Claude through a read-only triage MCP server, signed in with their own work account and without holding any production credentials. A second server lets staff use Claude in the ERP as themselves, never with more rights than its own UI gives; it handled about a thousand calls in its first week. Together they let customer service debug issues and file tickets without waiting on the small dev team, and developers use the same tools.
content.EasyOppSenior:
I joined EasyOpp's small team on a work-time and fleet management platform, moving from Rails to C#, .NET and Azure.

  • Payroll calculation engine redesign. Took over the calculation core from its original author in 2024 and redesigned it so that every payroll minute traces back to the time slot that produced it. Before, results existed only per shift, so nobody could see why a shift produced its numbers; calculation correctness went from a common support-ticket category to rare edge cases.
  • Simpler model, simpler workflow. In the same redesign two salary tables became one, and saving hours and calculating salaries went from several steps across two screens to one button.
content.Adalia:
I designed and built web applications, for customer projects across industries and for Adalia's own monitoring and evaluation system. I started as a junior developer and grew into running projects on my own: I was often the sole maintainer of several projects at once, and mentored the junior developers who joined after me.

  • A new system from scratch. For one customer I started a completely new system: the application structure in React and Rails, the data model, and user and permission management, laid down first as the foundation the other developers then built on.
  • Offline support. For another, I built offline support: data saved while offline syncs to the server once the connection returns. My master's thesis covered the same subject, including caching the app in the browser with service workers.

The main stack was Ruby on Rails, React and PostgreSQL, and I also configured services on AWS Fargate and Lambda and worked on a Node.js API.
content.Other:
My side projects are small products for my own family, in daily use rather than demos. In them I do the product design end to end: I write the brief, design the screens and scope each feature, and Claude Code writes the code, which I mostly don't read. Specs, tests and checks carry the safety instead. The AI workflow itself I mostly develop in my day job, where I spend far more time with these tools and the stakes call for reading the diff too. Lessons travel both ways: the side projects reuse what works at work, and now and then something learned at home goes back.

Two lessons so far. Building a new app with AI is now fast and easy, but what to build and how it should work only becomes clear once someone uses it, so the real product work starts after the first version. And a repo's AI tooling needs upkeep like code: as the apps, the models and the tools change, I update and prune CLAUDE.md and the other docs so they stay correct and small enough to keep every session fast.

  • Family Planner. Built for a parent who studies full time with three small kids at home, whose study time was whatever was left over and never visible in advance. It reads the family's calendars, applies our own planning rules and shows ahead of time when the study blocks are and how they divide between deadlines, warning early when something won't fit. It started as a one-page brief: the problem, the core loop and what to leave out, such as AI inside the app, since planning help comes through Claude Desktop. I drew several screen directions as Claude mockups, chose between them and kept every decision in the repo. Each feature is then a written spec, built in one Claude Code session and tested against the spec in another. Started in late October 2026 and already in use.
  • Perheraha. Family finances built around one low-friction monthly routine instead of daily logging: spending, net worth, subscriptions and accounts across several banks in one place. Through its MCP server, Claude Desktop runs that routine against the app's own database, importing statements, sorting them and spotting refunds, with a dry run and a backup before every write, and balances change only when explicitly set. Real use keeps finding the rules: when a learned category rule filed refunds wrongly, the fix became a required parameter, so no later code path can forget it. No cloud backend: the data stays on our own devices.
  • Chore app. For kids who can't read yet, so everything works through pictures, taps and sounds: they tap a finished chore and earn collectible animals and vehicles that fill themed books and a small world. Scope and architecture are written down before each milestone, so sessions don't drift from them. The family's phones hold real progress, so updates are built never to wipe data, and after a bug that only the release build showed, anything network-related is verified on a release build on a device.

Family Planner runs on TypeScript and Cloudflare Workers, the other two on Flutter with local-first SQLite. Earlier I also published Sleep Clock to the Play Store, a small utility I built as a React PWA.

content.AIAssisted:
Most of my code is now written with Claude Code, so my work has moved to the system around it. When code is cheap to produce, the expensive parts are a clear spec, a review that catches what is subtly wrong, and the architecture calls a model can't make for you.

  • Spec, build and test in separate sessions. A feature starts as a written spec that I scope myself. A fresh session implements it and stops at a draft pull request, and another fresh session tests it against the spec in a browser on its preview environment, so no session grades its own work.
  • Staged review. The review flow exists to prepare a human approval, not to automate it. It settles the structure before anyone reads the lines: for a change that adds a new pattern, the intended behaviour is agreed on the ticket before the build, an independent architecture pass compares the change with the closest existing code, and a review packet gives the reviewer a reading order and the trade-offs worth a conscious ack. How many stages run depends on the stakes: a bugfix goes straight to the code-level pass, which is either a triaged self-review or an automatic line review. AI recommends and prepares; a person approves, and never their own work.
  • Rules as checks, not prose. Conventions that live only in instruction files get broken quietly once AI multiplies the number of pull requests, so I turn each rule into a build or test check. Existing violations go on an allowlist that can only shrink: new code meets the rule from day one and old debt is counted down. Before enforcing a check, I replay it against recent real pull requests to find false positives.
  • Small context, knowledge in the repo. Instructions are split by area and load only when matching files are touched. Knowledge that lived in one developer's private AI memory moved into the repo's docs, where teammates and every session can see it. Those docs are maintained like code: as the product, the models and the tools change, I update and prune them so they stay correct and small.

My side projects run on the same spec, build and test loop. Most of this workflow is developed at work, where I use these tools the most, and lessons move both ways between the two.
content.Product:
When code is cheap to produce, building the wrong thing becomes the main cost. A first version is quick to make, but what to build and how it should work only becomes clear once people use it, so I treat a release as the start of the product work, not the end.

  • Mockups before code. Every recent UI modernization started as Claude mockups. I ask for alternatives or a fresh redesign, and a design that holds up goes straight into implementation. Designs go to the dev team, and sometimes customer service or a customer, before anything is built. A mockup rarely draws much feedback, though. The real feedback comes from use.
  • Real use decides. Before I built tiered paid breaks, a customer confirmed they wanted option B; once they saw it working, they wanted A after all, so it changed. I built our customizable reporting tool before AI, so that anyone could build their own reports. It worked, but with so many buttons and options it never felt easy, so the redesign brought ready-made presets and a simpler UI, reworked over several mockup rounds until it no longer felt intimidating. Customer-defined mobile forms, which I designed from the data model up, show the other side: about 15 customers now fill in hundreds of forms a month.
  • Design for how people actually work. I start from the tool people already use. Planners who keep rosters in Excel got a planning table that works like one, with range selection and copy and paste, where a paste across thousands of cells applies all or nothing. With team-scoped editing rights, out-of-scope cells show as read-only instead of letting people run into an error.
  • Craft and accessibility. The web and mobile apps share design tokens, so they look like one product, and the dark theme never flashes the wrong colours on load. Colours were chosen by measured contrast: the brand green failed with white text, so buttons use a darker shade.
  • A product check in every review. In every pull request a preview can show, a separate Claude session uses the change in a browser and checks each claim in the ticket, so a change is judged by how it works, not only by how its code reads. A new feature also gets a human pass on the preview, without reading the code, that ends in proceed, reshape or kill.
content.Guardrails:
An agent with access to real systems is useful only if its mistakes can't do damage, so I put the limits where a model can't talk its way past them: in permissions, not prompts.

  • Read-only triage for the whole team. An MCP server lets anyone on the team investigate production through Claude. They sign in with their own work account, and the server holds the production and vendor credentials so nobody else has to. Read-only access and masked secrets are enforced by database permissions, so no prompt can widen them, and every call is logged under the person who made it.
  • Acting as the signed-in person. Through the ERP's MCP server, staff use Claude as themselves: every tool runs with that person's rights, never more than the ERP's own UI gives, and every call is logged.
  • Safe writes to personal data. In my family finance app, Claude Desktop works on the app's own database through an MCP server, with dry runs and a backup before every write.
content.Architecture:
Designing data models and system architecture is the part of the work I find most rewarding, and it matters more now that code is cheap to generate: a model writes whatever the design allows, so the design has to be right. I think carefully upstream so the downstream work stays simple.

  • Let the model absorb variation. I design for the variation customers will bring instead of writing code for each case. One payroll engine serves several collective labor agreements with no per-agreement code, and customers build their own mobile forms as templates.
  • Store the inputs, derive the rest. A recurring shift is one row expanded at read time, not a set of copies to keep in sync. Eco-driving scores cache the raw counters, never the scores, so the scoring formula has changed twice without recomputing history.
  • Make every result traceable. Every payroll minute traces back to the time slot that produced it, so a wrong number can be explained and fixed.
  • Say what is unknown. A value that can't be observed is stored as missing, not as zero, so a truck that can't report something doesn't get a bad score for it.
  • Invariants in the schema. What must always hold is enforced in the database with constraints and indexes, not trusted to application code that an agent may rewrite tomorrow.
content.Production:
In a small team I own what ships, so I change production in steps that can be checked and reversed.

  • Rehearse, then run in parallel. Big moves are rehearsed on dev and test first, and the new path runs beside the old one and is validated against real data before the switch.
  • Flip, watch, delete. Old code is retired by turning it off by default, watching that nothing still uses it, and only then deleting it.
  • Measure before fixing. Metrics first, then a canary. A slow database at low load turned out to be waiting on disk, not CPU, which changed the fix.
  • Fix the invariant, not the symptom. When a race could create duplicate records, the fix went into the schema as a unique index.
content.Stack:
Knowing a stack well is what lets me review generated code in it and see when a solution is subtly wrong. These are the ones I know best.

  • React and TypeScript. Almost ten years, since the start of my career. Several apps built from scratch, including this site.
  • C# and .NET. Backends at EasyOpp since 2023: web APIs with Entity Framework Core, SignalR for real-time updates, NUnit.
  • Azure. App Service, Functions, Azure SQL, Storage and SignalR, all deployed with Bicep. Earlier AWS (Fargate, Lambda) at Adalia.
  • Databases. SQL Server and Azure SQL today, PostgreSQL before: schema design, indexing and Query Store.
  • AI tooling. Claude Code, the Claude API and MCP servers, plus the skills and GitHub Actions behind the review flow.
  • Flutter and Dart. Side projects in daily use at home, with Riverpod, Drift over SQLite and Supabase sync.
  • Ruby on Rails. Six years at Adalia, as an API for React frontends and as a classic MVC app, tested with RSpec.
